items.title: A BJP worker in Uttarakhand objected. Voters in Kichha who never knew him are off the roll
items.summary: This is part 2 of Newslaundry’s investigation into voter deletions in Kichha, Uttarakhand. A BJP booth-level agent filed Form 7 objections that he said were accepted on ECI’s directions. Here, we speak to voters whose names are missing from the final roll. In Sirauli Kalan, a Muslim-dominated urban locality in the Kichha assembly constituency in Uttarakhand, Newslaundry met Kulsum, a 25-year-old mother of two, against whom Rajesh Tiwari, a BJP booth-level agent (BLA), filed a Form 7 objection and whose name was subsequently deleted from the final voter list. She didn’t even know her name had been deleted from the voter list until we met her. Against her name, Tiwari's objection was “Already Enrolled” (in another state as a voter). items.title: Uttarakhand ERO refused BJP worker’s bulk Form 7 objections. After ECI complaint, 5,359 were accepted
items.summary: In August, Newslaundry reported how bulk Form 7 applications were being used to target voters in Uttarakhand during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. Across constituencies in the state, thousands of Form 7 applications were filed by BJP workers, with most objections targeting Muslim voters. In Kichha constituency of Udham Singh Nagar district, our investigation found that 4,390 names that appeared in the draft electoral roll were missing from the final roll released on October 3. Of these, around 670 were voters against whom Form 7 objections had been filed in August, 509 of them by Rajesh Tiwari, a booth-level agent (BLA) associated with the BJP. Of the 6,884 Form 7 objections accepted in Kichha, 5,359 were Tiwari’s. He is a close associate of former MLA Rajesh Shukla and BJP district cell coordinator of Udham Singh Nagar. Speaking to Newslaundry , Tiwari claimed that the local electoral registration officer (ERO) initially refused to accept the bulk Form 7 objections, saying there was no such provision in Election Commission of India (ECI) rules. items.title: Kerala High Court changes its internship policy; only those in final 2 years of LL.B allowed
items.summary: The Kerala High Court has revised its 2026 internship policy, introducing new rules governing applications, entry passes, attendance and the conduct of law students interning at the High Court. The revised policy, titled ' Internship Policy for the High Court of Kerala-2026 (Amended), ' was notified on October 17 and lays down detailed procedures governing internships at the High Court. Clause 6(a) of the policy states that "o nly students in the last two years of their law courses shall be eligible to undergo an internship in the High Court. " The restriction, however, does not apply to internships permitted at the discretion of judges. The policy applies to law students interning under High Court judges and other sections of the Court as well as offices including those of the Advocate General, Additional Solicitor General, Director General of Prosecution, Deputy Solicitor General, Kerala State Legal Services Authority, Mediation Centre, Bar Council of Kerala and other advocates. For internship opportunities under the judges, applications will be processed only after obtaining their consent.
